# Shifting attention to orient or avoid: a unifying account of the tail of the striatum and its dopaminergic inputs

**Authors:** Isobel Green; Ryunosuke Amo; Mitsuko Watabe-Uchida

**Affiliations:** Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Center for Brain Science, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA

## Abstract

The tail of the striatum (TS) is increasingly recognized as a unique subdivision of the striatum, characterized by its dense sensory inputs and projections received from a distinct group of dopamine neurons. Separate lines of research have characterized the functional role of TS, and TS-projecting dopamine neurons, in three realms: saccadic eye movement towards valuable visual stimuli; tone-guided choice between two options; and defensive responses to threatening stimuli. We propose a framework for reconciling these diverse roles as varied implementations of a conserved response to salient stimuli, with dopamine in TS providing a teaching signal to promote quick attentional shifts that facilitate stimulus-driven orientation and/or avoidance.

## Introduction

Historically, the striatum has been classified into several divisions based on connectivity and function [1]. Recent studies in rodents have started to re-appreciate one of these divisions, the ‘tail of the striatum’ (TS), named for its anatomical homology to the caudate tail (CDt) in primates [2–7]. Here, we first review the anatomy of TS and its connectivity, then discuss evidence implicating TS and TS-projecting dopamine neurons in diverse behavioral functions. Finally, we suggest that these apparently disparate accounts of TS function can be understood in a common framework, in which TS identifies physically salient stimuli and directs a rapid attentional shift to promote stimulus-responsive behavior necessary for survival.

## Anatomical features of TS

Anatomically, TS is considered to be the sensory domain of the striatum. TS receives dense projections from visual and auditory cortices and thalamus, but unlike adjacent dorsolateral striatum (DLS), receives few projections from somatosensory and motor cortices [3,4,8–11] (Figure 1B). Unlike the dorsomedial striatum (DMS), TS receives few projections from the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), yet receives strong projections from the temporal association cortex (TeA), a multi-modal object recognition area. This suggests segregation of information flow between anterior and posterior caudate (DMS and TS, respectively). TS receives projections from a unique group of dopamine neurons spanning the caudolateral substantia nigra pars compacta (clSNc) and the substantia nigra pars lateralis (SNL) (Figure 1A). These dopamine neurons in turn receive inputs distinct from dopamine neurons projecting to the rest of the striatum, including the zona incerta (ZI) and the intermediate layer of the superior colliculus (SC), the multi-modal integration center for orienting and avoidance [5,12].

Like other striatal subregions, TS is mainly composed of two types of projection neurons: D1 receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons (D1-MSNs) and D2-MSNs [13–15]. D1-MSNs primarily target the caudo-dorsolateral substantia nigra reticulata (cdlSNr) and SNL, (‘direct pathway’); D2-MSNs target the caudoventral globus pallidus (cvGP or cvGPe) which in turn targets cdlSNr/SNL (‘indirect pathway’) [13,16]. The cvGP also targets other regions including the caudal thalamic reticular nucleus (cTRN), a visual and auditory processing center [17]. The cdlSNr/SNL sends dense projections to superior colliculus (SC) and inferior colliculus (IC), as well as periaqueductal gray (PAG) and cuneiform nucleus (CnF) [18,19]. Interconnected with various perceptual and sensorimotor brain areas, TS is well-positioned to link perception and action.

## Role of the CDt in Directed Eye Movements

TS is considered a homologue of CDt in primates, as both regions receive strong projections from auditory, visual and object cortices and thalamus, and few projections from prefrontal areas [3,4,8]. Consistent with its dense visual connectivity, stimulus-directed saccades robustly engage CDt and adjacent caudoventral putamen (putamen tail; PUTt). Electrophysiological recordings in macaques performing saccades to visual objects on a screen (Figure 2A) showed that CDt/PUTt neurons exhibit sharp stimulus selectivity and relatively large spatial selectivity [2,20,21], similar to visual responses in higher sensory cortical areas [20]. Notably, CDt neurons increased their activity to a stimulus in their visual and spatial receptive field both when stimuli were presented in the periphery as animals maintained center-screen fixation (passive viewing), and immediately before a saccade when animals were permitted to saccade (free viewing). The response to visual stimuli during fixation suggests that responses in CDt are stimulus-associated and not necessarily motor-evoked [21]. Further supporting CDt’s role in stimulus-directed saccades, electrical stimulation of CDt or optogenetic activation of CDt terminals in cdlSNr induced contralateral saccades during free viewing [16,21]. Furthermore, after saccades to certain stimuli were consistently rewarded, CDt/PUTt neurons responded more to the reward-predicting stimuli, paralleling the monkey’s gaze bias [22,23].

Similar to CDt, putative CDt-projecting dopamine neurons in the clSNc, unlike many other dopamine neurons, responded to reward-associated stimuli in the contralateral hemifield, but they did not consistently respond to reward itself [24]. Reward-associated stimulus responses were resistant to extinction, leading to the hypothesis that CDt neurons and CDt dopamine signal “stable reward value” in contrast to “flexible reward value” in other striatal areas. However, the lack of reward responses in CDt dopamine is inconsistent with pure value signaling. Rather, CDt and clSNc dopamine neurons are activated by valued visual stimuli specifically, and CDt plays a role in saccades toward such stimuli.

## Roles for TS in Auditory Discrimination

The role of TS in tone-guided behavior is well-characterized in rodents (Figure 2B). Similar to visual stimulus selectivity in CDt neurons, TS activity encodes sound identity tonotopically [25–27]. Furthermore, when distinct tones were paired with reward at a left or right port, TS-projecting auditory cortex inputs responsive to the tone associated with contralateral reward were selectively potentiated [26]. TS activity during the tone encoded little information about upcoming choice [25] (but see [28]), and did not change when tone-port associations were reversed [25], suggesting that TS activity during tone, like visual-stimulus responses in monkeys, encodes sensory features rather than the next action. Accordingly, optogenetic activation of TS did not induce movement by itself, in contrast to optogenetic activation of DLS which caused contralateral turns [25,29]. However, when paired with a tone, optogenetic activation of either TS-projecting auditory cortical inputs or TS neurons biased port selection [25,28,30]. Supporting a role for TS in auditory-guided decisions, pharmacological or chemogenetic inhibition of either TS or projections to TS from auditory cortex or auditory thalamus significantly impaired performance [25,31]. Moreover, optogenetic inhibition of dopamine inputs to TS during tone presentation acutely impaired choice [32]. Taken together, these results suggest that TS and TS dopamine activity is important for either tone discrimination or tone-guided action selection, with further research needed to disambiguate these two possibilities.

## Roles for TS in avoidance of a threatening stimulus

Another line of work has demonstrated that TS-projecting dopamine neurons encode threatening stimuli. TS dopamine neurons are generally excited by physically salient (also conceivable as threatening) external stimuli such as tone, odor, air puff and aggressive conspecifics, but are not reliably excited by reward [33–35]. Moreover, they are not excited by other negative events such as reward omission and bitter water, so they are unlikely to signal negative value or motivational value [34].

Ablation and optogenetic experiments have confirmed the importance of TS-projecting dopamine neurons in threat response. Ablation of these neurons impairs choice between two water ports with distinct outcomes: while control mice avoided a port that delivered water with an air puff, preferring a port dispensing only water, ablation mice did not avoid the same (Figure 2C); yet both groups were able to learn to avoid a port dispensing less water or water with a bitter taste [34]. Thus TS-projecting dopamine neurons facilitate avoidance of threatening stimuli but appear dispensable for reward value-based choice. Optogenetic experiments support this finding: during fear conditioning, optogenetic inhibition of TS-projecting dopamine neurons during a shock-predicting tone (or inhibiting TS D1-MSNs at tone or shock) impaired subsequent fear recall, measured by tone-induced freezing [29,36] (Figure 2D). Fear conditioning itself increased TS responses to the shock-predicting tone, an increase dependent on TS dopamine [36]. Finally, TS activation acutely increased freezing [37], suggesting that TS impacts action selection following a threat in addition to fear learning.

Further supporting a role for TS in threat-mediated behavior, TS-projecting dopamine neurons were strongly excited by a novel stimulus, and their responses persisted only if the stimulus was associated with a threat such as air puff [33,34] or electric shock [36,38]. In a more naturalistic setting, TS dopamine neurons were implicated in determining novel object avoidance [34,39,40] (Figure 2E). TS dopamine neurons were activated at the moment mice were closest to a novel object in each approach bout [34,39], and the magnitude of this response predicted individual variability in novel object exploration: while mice with intrinsically stronger TS dopamine activation tended to be more avoidant, those with ablation of TS-projecting dopamine neurons tended to be bolder [34,39]. These studies suggest that TS dopamine response to novel stimuli may determine whether the animal proceeds to future avoidance of novelty, potentially by setting stimulus-associated threat predictions. Interestingly, CDt neurons in monkeys also show robust responses to novel objects [21,41], although minimal data exists regarding responses of CDt-projecting dopamine neurons to novelty (but see [42]).

## Roles for TS in attentional shift and sensory representation

These varied roles of TS may appear incongruous: depending on the context, TS and TS dopamine are responsible for object-directed saccades, tone-guided choice, or threat avoidance (Figure 2). One possibility is that distinct subregions of TS, or different subpopulations of TS neurons and TS-projecting dopamine neurons, mediate each function. Alternatively, these apparently disparate roles may each be expressions of a common circuit function. We propose one such common framework, inspired by evolutionary perspectives [43–45]: TS promotes a quick (potentially sub-second) attentional shift (e.g., a saccade or covert monitoring) toward salient sensory information, facilitating subsequent behavioral responses such as sustained orientation or avoidance, depending on the nature of the stimulus (Figure 3). Notably, cdlSNr, directly downstream of CDt, is activated by both rewarding and threatening stimuli [42], and monkeys preferentially saccade towards novel or threatening objects as well as rewarding ones [46]. Thus, initial saccade preference, and tightly linked CDt activity, may be a readout for stimulus salience. The appearance of salient stimuli may first trigger CDt activity leading to saccades as an initial alerting response to stimulus salience, followed by further behavioral responses as needed, such as sustained orientation (tracking, pursuit) or avoidance.

Indeed, the anatomical position of TS suggests its alerting signal is well-poised to drive both orienting and avoidance behavior. One of the major projection targets of the TS-SNL pathway is the SC (Figure 1, Figure 3), an evolutionarily conserved region which mediates orienting and avoidance through distinct outputs. In the lamprey, for example, moderately salient (slow-looming) stimuli activate SC projections to the contralateral brainstem (“crossed” pathway) to produce stimulus-directed orienting, while highly salient (fast-looming) stimuli activate SC outputs to both contralateral and ipsilateral brainstem (“uncrossed pathway”), leading to less directed, evasive behavior [47]. In mice, optogenetic stimulation of the crossed pathway elicits quick contralateral orienting followed by contralateral turning, while optogenetic stimulation of the uncrossed pathway elicits quick upwards head movements, followed by defensive behaviors such as retreat and flight [48]. Across species, TS and TS dopamine activation likely influence the SC pathways engaged by salient stimuli and resulting behavior. Importantly, TS activity and behavioral response to the same stimuli may differ between species, with a stimulus’ physical salience/threat level determined by species-specific combinations of factors (e.g. stimulus location, movement and size) [43,47,49]. Through this framework, we can consider reward-associated stimuli in the object-saccade task as being moderately salient to monkeys, and thus engaging only the “crossed” pathway to trigger stimulus-directed orienting. Highly physically salient stimuli such as electric shock, air puff, looming stimuli and threat-predicting stimuli, on the other hand, may strongly engage the SC avoidance (“uncrossed”) pathway, which projects to IC, PAG and CnF (Figure 3), regions key for evasive responses [18,50]. Interestingly, SNL projects to IC, PAG, and CnF directly as well as indirectly (through SC), suggesting multiple routes to induce avoidance [18]. Moreover, SNL preferentially projects to medial and central SC, which monitor the upper visual field to mediate avoidance of airborne predators, but not to lateral SC, which monitors the ground for food [18,43]. Based on the close anatomical relationship between TS and brain areas involved in avoidance, and established roles for the SC in both orienting and avoidance, we propose that TS is specialized to promote a stimulus-guided attentional shift that facilitates subsequent orienting and/or avoidance behavior. Whether TS activity directly informs the decision to orient and/or avoid depending on salience level (our proposed model), or simply acts as a permissive signal for a decision formed elsewhere, requires further investigation.

The idea that TS circuitry facilitates orienting to moderately salient stimuli such as reward-predicting stimuli also accounts for the role of TS in tone-guided choice tasks. After extensive training, such tasks, which unnaturally pair a salient stimulus (tone) with a reward-associated location (port), may exploit an ancient TS circuit for orientation towards a stimulus: TS may drive attention towards the tone and facilitate subsequent orienting to the paired port (Figure 3). Because each TS neuron has both spatial and stimulus selectivity, TS neurons could gradually learn linked combinations of these features during intensive training, allowing TS to facilitate both attention to the tone and subsequent orientation towards an associated port. Alternatively, TS might be engaged not for turning itself, but for initial direction of attention towards the auditory stimulus, akin to the function of a saccade towards visual stimuli. This latter possibility, however, may be less consistent with findings that stimulation of TS neurons during tones induces a contralateral port bias [25,30,51].

Importantly, in parallel with its outputs to the brainstem for behavioral control, TS may also influence behavior by affecting sensory representation (Figure 3). A classical study mapping the structure of cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops found that CDt forms a loop structure back to TeA [6], suggesting a potential influence on object recognition. Furthermore, a recent study indicated that in perceptually-demanding tone discrimination tasks, TS regulates tone representation in the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN, ‘auditory thalamus’) via a cvGP-cTRN pathway [52,53] (Figure 1). Thus, manipulation of CDt/TS or TS dopamine in experimental settings may distort sensory representation and perception, which may cause a deficit in sensory discrimination itself, rather than or in addition to a deficit in action selection. Whether the same TS neurons regulate switches in attention and sensory representation remains to be seen.

## Roles for dopamine in TS: Reinforcement and modulation of attention

If the role of TS is to facilitate stimulus-guided action, be it orienting or avoidance, what is the role of dopamine in TS? Given its demonstrated role in fear learning [36,38], a strong possibility is that TS dopamine functions in a threatening context as a teaching signal, similar to the demonstrated role for dopamine in reward-based reinforcement learning [54] (Figure 4A). In this spirit, Akiti et al. proposed a simple threat-based reinforcement-learning model to account for the finding that TS dopamine underlies novelty avoidance, with TS dopamine signaling “threat prediction error”, instead of reward prediction error (RPE) classically proposed for dopamine [39]. Because it could be catastrophic for an animal to rely on actual experiences of harm to learn to predict potential threat, this model proposes that an animal may first use physical salience – e.g., stimulus size, intensity and movement – as an initial estimate of threat prediction (‘shaping bonus’) [55] (Figure 4B). This is consistent with the finding that TS dopamine activity is modulated by the intensity of novel stimuli from multiple modalities [5]. The initial estimate is later refined by experiences of salient events involving the object, and eventually converges to a more accurate prediction of net future salience associated with the stimulus [39]. In this sense, the dopamine teaching signal in TS can be interpreted as a more generalized ‘salience prediction error’, which may be used to train TS to predict future salience. Once the salience predicted by TS exceeds a predetermined avoidance threshold, animals may avoid the associated stimulus. Using this model to simulate threat prediction learning with dopamine in TS, the authors could account for complex temporal dynamics and individual variability in naturalistic interactions with a novel object. In short, TS dopamine may link primitive sensory features (physical salience) with behavioral avoidance. This idea is supported by a recent study, which found that TS dopamine release, the physical salience of a threatening stimulus, and stimulus avoidance rate are all correlated, and manipulation of TS dopamine bidirectionally modulated the link between physical salience and avoidance (Figure 4C) [15].

Compared to their well-defined role in avoidance, the precise role of CDt/TS dopamine in mediating object-reward or tone-port associations is controversial. For example, in auditory discrimination tasks, one study observed induction of a contralateral bias upon unilateral activation of dopamine axons [51], whereas another study observed no bias even with unilateral stimulation, leading the authors to pool unilateral and bilateral stimulation [56]. The discrepancy between these studies remains to be resolved in future work. In either case, the salience prediction error proposed to facilitate threat avoidance may be also used to learn orienting towards salient stimuli in a non-threatening environment. Through the lens of our proposed model (Figure 3), perturbations disrupting TS dopamine (thus altering salience prediction error) or TS neuron activity (thus altering the net future salience prediction) could impact initial attention to the guiding tone, subsequent port-orienting behavior, and/or resultant learning across the session.

Importantly, dopamine release in TS during cue presentation has also been shown to influence on-going choice behavior [32] and/or learning [36]. A recent study likewise found that ablation of TS-projecting dopamine neurons affects avoidance behavior from the very first trial, suggesting acute effects of TS dopamine in addition to effects on learning across trials [15]. These studies suggest that TS dopamine may acutely enhance TS signaling, influencing sensory representation and/or attentional control over a downstream orienting/avoidance pathway that results in both a bias in immediate choice in the current trial, and enhanced learning.

## Conclusion

The TS has been implicated in diverse domains, including visual orientation, tone-guided choice, and avoidance of threatening stimuli. We propose a general framework for understanding these varied functions, placing TS at the center of a circuit linking salient sensory stimuli to conserved action programs. Specifically, we propose that TS learns a prediction of future physical salience associated with stimuli and provides this information to ancient circuitry responsible for rapid control of attention to drive responsive action, especially orientation (upon moderate physical salience prediction) and/or avoidance (upon high physical salience prediction). We propose that TS dopamine functions as a teaching signal to facilitate this prediction. Future work is called for to understand how the proposed role of TS in attentional shift is implemented across varied contexts, whether distinct cell types or subareas within TS are differentially engaged depending on the task at hand, and how acute and learning effects of TS and TS dopamine activity are combined with information from other striatal subregions to facilitate balanced decision-making.

When mice were confronted with a novel object in an open arena, they first showed characteristic initial “risk assessment” behavior, followed by a profile of either object engagement or avoidance that varied considerably across mice. TS dopamine response to the object was correlated with the extent of avoidance, and ablation of TS dopamine neurons decreased avoidance, promoting engagement with the object. A threat-based reinforcement learning model, in which an initial estimate of threat prediction (‘shaping bonus’) is updated by threat prediction errors conveyed by TS dopamine, was able to capture the complex behavioral dynamics observed across mice.
